newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FORECAST-SingTel to post 12 pct net rise.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-SingTel to post 12 pct net rise.

text.p: Southeast Asia's biggest company, Singapore Telecommunications Ltd (SingTel), is set to post a 12 percent rise in net profit for 1996/97, reflecting growth in international calls and mobile phone use, analysts said on Thursday.

But the results, due out at 0900 GMT on Friday, may be the high water mark for the company and many analysts say profit growth is likely to decline from now on as competition at home and abroad erodes margins.

"This year's results will be up by around 12 percent," said John Chessher, regional telecoms analyst with Schroders in Singapore. "But next year will begin to show the effects of lower prices and smaller market share."

The latest poll of 34 securities houses by Edinburgh Financial Publishing's Estimate Directory forecasts SingTel's 1996/97 net profit at Singapore $1.67 billion (US$1.17 billion), up from S$1.49 billion a year ago.
The directory expects an 11 percent year-on-year rise in net for 1997/98 to S$1.86 billion.
A former state-run monopoly, SingTel was privatised in 1992 and has harvested rich rewards from its small but affluent captive market of business and retail customers.
But the cosy monopoly was broken in April this year when one rival, MobileOne (M1), entered the lucrative mobile phone market and three new pager serives were licensed.
M1 is a venture of Britain's Cable & Wireless, Hongkong Telecommunications, Singapore Press Holdings and Keppel Telecom.
From April 2000, SingTel will also face competition in its fixed-line telephone market and its has already begun to reduce international charges to keep up with falling global rates.

SingTel's weighted average international tariff rates have fallen to around S$1.70 per minute from S$2.02 in January 1996 and ING Baring's regional telecoms analyst Gautam Kapoor expects these to slip to S$1.67 by March 1998 and S$1.50 by March 1999.
Since international direct dialing (IDD) accounts for around 50 percent of the company's total revenue, these lower charges will inevitably eat into margins, he said.
"We see its IDD call revenue going up just 3.1 percent in the year to March 1997," Kapoor said.
He said the fastest growing income would still be from mobile phones and this revenue stream would expand by almost 22 percent in the current year.
Most analysts say SingTel is fairly well managed and expect operational costs to be held in check this year with a year-on-year rise of around 10 percent.
But they argue that the loss of the company's monopoly has still not been factored properly into the share price.
"At a stock price of S$2.54, SingTel appears to be over-valued on all parameters," said Kapoor. "We see a fair valuation at S$1.70-S$2.00 per share. We have a sell on it."
Other analysts agreed, saying the stock had retained a relatively high price due to its inclusion in influential stock market indices and possibly some political factors.
Singapore state investment company Temasek Holdings still owns 82 percent of SingTel, they noted.
"No one disputes the fact that it is over-valued, but it has stared coming down recently," said Chessher. "On a price earnings basis we end up with a valuation around S$1.50."
-- Singapore newsroom (65 8703199)
